8 Chemical reactions

8.1 Exothermic reactions

Key words: combustion · dissipate · exothermic reaction · fuel · oxidation reaction · preliminary work

Burning

When something burns, a chemical reaction takes place. Burning is a chemical reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen. In a burning reaction, there are energy changes.

The substance that reacts with oxygen is called a fuel. Fuels have a store of chemical energy. Charcoal, wood, coal, natural gas and oil are examples of fuels.

When the fuel burns, the chemical energy is changed to thermal, light and sound energy. The thermal, light and sound energy dissipate (spread out) into the surroundings.

Burning needs three things together. If any one of them is missing, the fuel will not burn.

Combustion is another term for burning.

When carbon burns, the atoms of carbon and oxygen join together in new ways.

When this happens, chemical energy is changed to thermal energy and the temperature rises. A chemical reaction in which thermal energy is given out is called an exothermic reaction.

Remember: in an exothermic reaction the temperature of the surroundings goes up, because energy is given out.

Burning other substances

Hydrogen can be used as a fuel in a model rocket. The combustion of hydrogen is an exothermic reaction. The hydrogen and the oxygen combine to form water.

When the atoms of hydrogen and oxygen rearrange themselves and combine together, energy is given out. This chemical energy is changed into kinetic, thermal, sound and light energy.

In this experiment, a large plastic soda bottle filled with hydrogen and air is attached to a string across the room. The stopper in the bottle has wires that allow a spark to be generated. The hot spark provides the energy to start the reaction. The hydrogen and oxygen react together. The reaction gives out a lot of energy and the stopper is pushed out, so the bottle shoots along the string.

The reactions of other substances burning in air are also exothermic reactions. An example is burning magnesium, which produces magnesium oxide.

Energy is given out as heat and light as the magnesium and oxygen atoms rearrange themselves.

When a substance burns, it combines with oxygen and a new substance called an oxide is formed. Any reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen is an oxidation reaction.

Exothermic reactions without burning

Not every exothermic reaction is a burning reaction. Potassium reacts with water without any flame being applied.

Water is made up of particles containing atoms of hydrogen and oxygen. In the potassium and water reaction, the bonds between the atoms of oxygen and hydrogen in the water break. The atoms rearrange to form the products potassium hydroxide and hydrogen. Stored chemical energy is changed to thermal energy, which dissipates into the environment.

If you add magnesium to dilute hydrochloric acid the test tube gets hot. This reaction is an exothermic one.

Measuring the rise in temperature during a reaction

Sofia and Marcus each measured 10 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid into a test tube and measured the temperature. Then they each added an identical piece of magnesium ribbon to their test tube of acid. When the reaction stopped, they each measured the temperature again.

The bigger the temperature rise, the more chemical energy has been changed to thermal energy. Before a full investigation it is useful to do some preliminary work — a quick trial run that shows whether the quantities and the method will give results you can use.

8.2 Endothermic reactions

Key words: endothermic process · endothermic reaction

Reactions that take energy in

Some chemical reactions absorb thermal energy from their surroundings and change it to chemical energy stored in the chemical bonds. These are called endothermic reactions.

When an endothermic reaction takes place, the temperature at the end of the reaction is lower than that at the start of the reaction.

You can show this with citric acid (or lemon juice) and sodium hydrogen carbonate:

  1. Place some citric acid or lemon juice in a test tube so that it is about half full.
  2. Measure and record the temperature.
  3. Add three spatulas of sodium hydrogen carbonate and stir. Do not use the thermometer to do this.
  4. Measure and record the temperature.

This is the word equation for the reaction:

sodium hydrogen carbonate + citric acid → sodium citrate + water + carbon dioxide

During this reaction, thermal energy is absorbed from the surroundings and stored in the form of chemical bonds. So the surroundings have a lower temperature and the test tube feels cooler.

If you eat sherbet sweets, this reaction takes place in your mouth. The sherbet is a mixture of dry citric acid and sodium hydrogen carbonate. When you eat the sweets, these substances dissolve in your saliva and react together. This gives a cool 'fizzy' feeling in your mouth (the surroundings), which is refreshing.

Endothermic processes

Not every change that takes energy in is a reaction.

If you place some water in a beaker and then stir in three spatulas of potassium chloride, you will find that the beaker gets cold. In this case, no chemical reaction has taken place. No new products are formed — the potassium chloride has just dissolved. A solution of potassium chloride has been formed, in which potassium chloride is the solute and water is the solvent.

When potassium chloride dissolves in water, thermal energy is absorbed from the surroundings. This is why the beaker feels cold. This is an endothermic process.

Ice melting is another endothermic process. Thermal energy is absorbed from the surroundings as the solid ice changes to liquid water.

The particles in the ice are lined up in rows and can only vibrate about fixed positions — they cannot move around inside the ice. The forces between the particles are strong. As the particles absorb thermal energy from the surroundings, they vibrate more and more. When the particles have enough energy, they can move and overcome the forces holding them in place. The particles can now slide past one another, and the water is in a liquid state.

Remember: a reaction makes new substances; a process such as dissolving or melting does not. Both can be exothermic or endothermic.

Exothermic or endothermic?

ExothermicEndothermic
Energygiven out to the surroundingstaken in from the surroundings
Temperature of surroundingsrisesfalls
Examplesburning, metal + acid, calcium + watercitric acid + sodium hydrogen carbonate, dissolving potassium chloride, ice melting

A polystyrene cup is a good container for this kind of experiment, because it is a poor conductor and keeps the energy change inside the cup.

When you plan an experiment like this, you also need to think about how accurate and how precise your measurements are.

Using exothermic reactions

Some exothermic reactions are used to produce self-heating cans of food or drink. A can of self-heating food contains two chemicals, which are in separate compartments. When you open the can, the two chemicals mix with each other and react, and the reaction warms up the food or drink.

The chemicals used are calcium oxide and water:

calcium oxide + water → calcium hydroxide

These cans can be very useful if you are in a remote area, or in an emergency when there is no power, or when you are camping. They are expensive to produce, because the compartments must be sealed from one another and from the food so that it does not become contaminated. There have also been problems with the food not being heated evenly.

Using endothermic processes

People sometimes use ice packs when they injure themselves. These packs are stored in a fridge or freezer until they are needed. When the ice pack is placed on the injured area, heat from this area is transferred to the ice pack and the ice melts. The injured area is cooled, and this often prevents it from swelling up. After it has been used, the ice pack can go back into the freezer to be used again.

Some 'ice' packs are made from substances that undergo an endothermic process when they mix together. These packs can be used even when you don't have a fridge or freezer. The pack has two compartments inside, each with a different substance — usually ammonium nitrate and water. When you push on the pack and break the compartment containing ammonium nitrate, the water mixes with it and the ammonium nitrate begins to dissolve. This is an endothermic process, so the temperature drops.

8.3 Metals and their reactions with oxygen

Key words: collapses · inert · prevent · reactive · rusts

Metals and oxygen

Many metals react with oxygen if they get hot enough. When you look carefully at the reactions of metals with oxygen, it is possible to identify which metals are more reactive. For example, magnesium is more reactive than iron because magnesium reacts more quickly than iron.

This reaction between metals and oxygen is an oxidation reaction:

metal + oxygen → metal oxide

You can compare metals by heating a small piece of each one in a Bunsen flame and recording what you see.

Some metals react very quickly with oxygen without even being heated. When pieces of sodium, potassium or calcium are taken from their containers, they appear dull. When the pieces are cut, the surface is shiny. The shiny surface soon becomes dull because the metal reacts with the oxygen in the air, and the surface becomes covered with a new substance — the oxide of the metal.

These metals are so reactive that they have to be stored under oil to prevent them reacting. The layer of metal oxide on the surface prevents any more of the metal from reacting with the air or water vapour.

Some metals, such as gold, do not react with oxygen. They are generally unreactive and are described as inert. Silver reacts slowly with the air: if a silver object is not cleaned it goes black over time, as silver oxide is formed.

The reaction between iron and oxygen

When iron is left in damp air it rusts. The iron reacts with oxygen to form an orange-brown solid, called iron oxide, otherwise known as rust.

This is not a very useful reaction, because it means that the iron changes and no longer has the same properties. A strong iron girder can become rusted and fall apart, which could mean that a building collapses.

What causes iron to rust?

A new iron nail is placed in each of four test tubes, as in the diagram.

TubeWhat is in itAir?Water?
1nail only, open to the airyesno
2water, nail half in the water, open to the airyesyes
3calcium chloride, which absorbs water, so the air is dryyesno
4boiled water with a layer of oil on top, which stops air enteringnoyes

After a few weeks the experiment looks like this.

Only the nail in tube 2 rusts badly. The reaction between iron and oxygen only takes place when both water and oxygen are present. The water is not part of the equation, but it is needed for the reaction to happen. The reaction takes a long time to happen — iron is not very reactive with oxygen.

How can iron be protected?

Rusting can be slowed down or stopped by keeping air and water away from the iron surface.

8.4 Reactions of metals with water

Key words: reactivity · sandpaper

Reactions of sodium and potassium with water

Sodium reacts vigorously with water. Potassium is even more reactive than sodium. So much thermal energy is generated that the hydrogen gas produced in the reaction catches fire.

In these two reactions the metal reacted with water to produce hydrogen and the metal hydroxide:

metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen

Reactions of other metals with water

Some other metals react less vigorously with water — for example, calcium and magnesium.

To compare metals fairly, take a small piece of each metal, use sandpaper to clean the surface, and place it into a test tube of water. You may need to leave the metal to react for some time. If nothing happens, you could try testing the metal again, this time using hot water.

In the experiment shown in the diagram, a piece of calcium has been placed at the bottom of a beaker and covered with water. A filter funnel has been placed upside down over the metal. The gas given off is collected in a test tube by the displacement of water.

Metals and steam

Some of the metals that do not react with water may react with steam. Even magnesium will react more rapidly with steam than with water.

In the reaction shown here, magnesium is heated. From time to time, the heat is directed at the ceramic wool. The ceramic wool has been soaked in water, which when heated produces steam. In this reaction the magnesium reacts with water, which is in the form of a gas. Magnesium oxide and hydrogen are formed:

magnesium + water (g) → magnesium oxide + hydrogen

The (g) after water indicates it is water in the form of a gas, in this case steam. Steam is formed by boiling water and is very hot, whereas water vapour is made up of water particles in the air at lower temperatures.

Some metals, such as gold, do not react with water at all. Putting the metals in order of how strongly they react gives their order of reactivity.

8.5 Reactions of metals with dilute acids

Key words: reagents · salt

A familiar reaction

You will probably remember the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid. This is the word equation for this reaction:

magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

Magnesium chloride is an example of a salt. When a metal reacts with an acid, the products are a salt and hydrogen:

metal + acid → salt + hydrogen

Planning an investigation

Sofia and Marcus have been asked to investigate the reactions of metals with acids. They need to decide which of the equipment and reagents in the laboratory they need, to enable them to carry out the investigation safely.

The more reactive the metal, the faster the bubbles of hydrogen are produced. Comparing the bubbles in each tube puts the metals in order of reactivity.

Comparing fuels

The same idea of a fair test is used when comparing how much thermal energy different fuels give out. Each fuel heats the same volume of water, and the rise in temperature is measured.

Summary checklist

  • I can describe what happens in an exothermic reaction.
  • I can explain that burning (combustion) is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen.
  • I can state what is needed for combustion to take place.
  • I can explain what an oxidation reaction is.
  • I can list some chemical reactions that are endothermic.
  • I can explain the difference between an endothermic reaction and an endothermic process.
  • I can describe some uses of exothermic and endothermic reactions and processes.
  • I can plan an investigation and carry it out safely.
  • I can describe the reactions of some metals with oxygen.
  • I can compare how reactive some metals are with oxygen.
  • I can describe the conditions needed for iron to rust and how rusting can be prevented.
  • I can describe the reactions of some metals with water and with steam.
  • I can compare how reactive some metals are with water.
  • I can describe the reactions of some metals with dilute acid.
  • I can write word equations for the reactions of metals with oxygen, water and acid.
